lesson.title: The Neutron: Nuclear Glue Without a Charge
lesson.summary: Neutrons are electrically neutral nuclear particles that add mass and stability to an atom's nucleus without affecting its chemical identity.
lesson.body:
Alongside every proton in an atomic nucleus sits, in nearly all elements heavier than ordinary hydrogen, at least one neutron. A neutron has almost the same mass as a proton, about 1.675 times 10 to the negative 27 kilograms, or roughly 1.009 atomic mass units, but it carries no electric charge at all. This single difference, zero charge instead of positive charge, gives the neutron a very different role in the atom. Where the proton determines identity, the neutron mostly determines stability and mass, without changing which element the atom belongs to.

Why does an atom need neutrons at all? Protons alone would repel each other fiercely, since like charges push apart, and that repulsion grows stronger the closer the protons are packed. Neutrons dilute that repulsion by adding extra strong-force attraction between nuclear particles without adding any extra electrical repulsion. This is why heavier elements, which pack more protons into the nucleus, need proportionally more neutrons to stay stable. Hydrogen's most common form has zero neutrons and one proton, a nucleus small enough to hold together on proton attraction alone. Uranium-238, by contrast, needs 146 neutrons to help hold together its 92 protons, and even then the nucleus is only marginally stable, which is why uranium is radioactive.

Because neutrons carry no charge, changing the neutron count in a nucleus does not change the atom's identity or its number of electrons, and therefore does not change its basic chemical behavior. Two atoms of the same element with different neutron counts are called isotopes, a concept built directly on understanding what protons fix and what neutrons leave free to vary. Carbon-12, the standard reference isotope for atomic mass, has six protons and six neutrons. Carbon-14, used in radiocarbon dating, still has six protons, but carries eight neutrons instead, giving it a heavier, less stable nucleus that slowly decays over thousands of years.

A worked example shows how to find neutron count directly. Chlorine has atomic number 17, meaning every chlorine atom has 17 protons. The common isotope chlorine-35 has a mass number of 35. Since mass number equals the number of protons plus neutrons, the neutron count is 35 minus 17, which equals 18 neutrons. The less common isotope chlorine-37 has mass number 37, so its neutron count is 37 minus 17, or 20 neutrons. Both isotopes are still chlorine, both have 17 protons, and both behave almost identically in chemical reactions, but they have measurably different masses because of those extra two neutrons.

Neutrons were discovered later than protons and electrons, identified by James Chadwick in 1932 when he showed that a mysterious radiation emitted by beryllium bombarded with alpha particles consisted of neutral particles with roughly the mass of a proton. That discovery completed the basic three-particle picture of the atom and made it possible to explain why atoms of the same element can have different masses, setting up the ideas of mass number and isotopes that follow directly from neutron count.
